newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Nigerians push Sierra Leone troops from airport.
newsitem.headline: Nigerians push Sierra Leone troops from airport.

text.p: Sierra Leone's army rulers said on Thursday their forces pulled back from Freetown international airport after heavy clashes with Nigerian troops there.
In further trouble for the government, students demanding that the military step down from power vowed to go ahead with street protests despite threats of a crackdown by authorities.
Heavy shelling overnight sparked panic in the capital where Nigerian-led West African forces are confronting soldiers who toppled the elected president, Ahmad Tejan Kabbah, on May 25.
Junta chief of staff Brigadier Samuel Koroma told Reuters Nigerian troops holding the airport bombarded his forces with mortar fire for more than six hours up to dawn on Thursday.
"Our forces have been pulled back to Port Loko about 35 miles (55 km) from the airport," Koroma said.
Nigerian troops are the backbone of the Economic Community of West Africa Monitoring Group (ECOMOG) whose main contingent is based in neighbouring Liberia.
The chief of staff did not give the position of his troops when the clash broke out, saying only that "our men had no contact with the Nigerians yesterday".
But a clandestine pro-Kabbah radio, believed to be based at the airport under Nigerian protection, said junta troops and rebel allies forming the so-called People's Army were to blame.
"Troops of the People's Army attacked the ECOMOG troops at Lungi International Airport last night but ECOMOG wiped them out," the radio said on Thursday.
There was no immediate comment from the Nigerians.
The two sides have clashed sporadically since a failed June 2 attempt by Nigerian troops to reverse the coup and remove junta leader Major Johnny Paul Koroma.

Scores of people died in fighting last month around a smaller airport at Jui, east of Freetown. Tension has been high since the breakdown of talks on July 31 between junta envoys and West African foreign ministers on resolving the crisis.
The foreign ministers from Nigeria, Ghana, Ivory Coast and Guinea began emergency talks in the Ghanaian capital Accra on Thursday to consider the next step.

It was their first meeting since negotiations broke down in Ivory Coast after the army announced it would retain power for four years. The announcement ruled out the immediate return to power of Kabbah, exiled in neighbouring Guinea.

But regional sanctions imposed on Sierra Leone after the coup forced Koroma last week to announce his willingness to resume talks. A junta delegation met Guinean President Lansana Conte in Conakry last weekend to seek a new roundtable.

ECOMOG is enforcing a crushing sea, land and air embargo imposed by the Economic Community of West African States to force the military out. Food and fuel are running short and the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organisation gave a warning on Thursday of imminent famine.

The coup, condemned by the United Nations and the Organisation of African Unity, sparked widespread looting and the flight of the business community, mostly Lebanese. Shops, banks and businesses remain closed.
The National Union of Sierra Leone Students said on Thursday it would defy a police ban on a planned march on Monday to demand an end to army rule.

"No threats or intimidation will stop us protesting against the junta," a student leader, who asked not to be identified, told reporters. "We want them to step down and Kabbah to return as the legitimate president."
